findings.F1: Sense 1 pattern 'verb + to-infinitive' is wrong for modal must (bare infinitive).
findings.F2: Obligation example 'You must hand in your homework by Friday' sits under the deduction sense.
findings.F3: Usage note uses the banned abbreviation 'e.g.'.
findings.F4: Fixed speaker comment 'I must say / I must admit' is not covered.
findings.F5: Irritated questions 'Must you always...?' are not covered.
findings.F6: Strong recommendation or invitation use ('You must try the cake') is not covered.
findings.F7: Sense 1 compare note on have to restates the sense explanation.
findings.F8: see_also repeats have-v and should-modal already given as compare links.
findings.F9: Pronunciation note respelling 'muhst' for the weak form is identical to the full form.
findings.F10: Cannot as the opposite of deductive must is stated in explanation, compare note, and adaptation.semantic.
findings.F11: The no-past-form / had to fact is repeated in explanation, usage note, learner errors, and adaptation.grammar.
findings.F12: Must not versus don't have to is repeated in usage note, learner errors, and adaptation.grammar.
findings.F13: Saying must has no future and to use will have to misleads; must refers to the future freely.
findings.F14: shall-modal is a poor synonym of must for learners (formal or legal obligation only).
findings.F15: Phrase 'if you must' explanation merely restates its definition.

missed: adaptation.semantic says the opposite of deductive must is 'cannot, not must not', but in American English deductive 'must not' (She must not be home; they must not have heard) is common and standard.
